first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are directly addressable by the onboarding path, and memory_86 plus memory_31 are the load-bearing beliefs for that choice. But both were consolidated on proxy outcomes (completion rate, first-week activation, time-to-value), not on sustainable long-term qualified revenue, so they are consequential yet insufficiently supported for the stated objective — exactly the triage criterion. I pull memory_86 first to see whether the original record tracked retention/qualified revenue downstream or stopped at completion, and whether the 'shortening' removed steps that also served qualification. I pull memory_73 second because promotional pricing is the loudest alternative under competitor pressure and is the highest downstream-risk option: 'acquisition and revenue lift' is a short-horizon signal that can conceal margin erosion, discount-anchoring, and a cohort of price-sensitive accounts with poor retention — if the archive shows no retention/LTV measurement, that direction should stay off the table this week rather than be chosen reactively. memory_31 is not verified because it is redundant with memory_86 for direction-setting, though its field-cutting mechanism is precisely the lead-quality hazard I want memory_86's record to speak to. Downstream value risk: an onboarding/signup simplification that lifts activation counts can simultaneously degrade lead qualification data and admit lower-intent accounts, inflating activation while flattening qualified revenue — so the experiment must be instrumented with qualified-pipeline and 60/90-day retention guardrails, not completion rate alone, and I will treat a completion-only win as unconverted. If memory_86's record turns out to be proxy-only with no revenue-quality follow-through, I will drop to a small guarded test rather than spend the slot at full scale. Chasing the competitor on price is the reactive move; repairing the funnel that is measurably degrading is the one that compounds.

mid.rationale: The archive resolves both questions in the direction that settles this cycle. exp_86 is stronger than the consolidated summary suggested: it carried retention +3% at 30 days alongside completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days, so the onboarding win is not purely a proxy-only result — it survived at least one downstream check. exp_73 is the decisive negative: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% sat on top of 30-day retention -12%, and the original record explicitly warns against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. That is the exact failure mode I flagged — a short-horizon revenue number concealing a cohort that does not survive first renewal. Under a sustainable-long-term-qualified-revenue objective, promotional_pricing is now affirmatively ruled out, not merely deprioritized, even though it is the direct answer to the competitor's move. So: spend the slot on shortening the onboarding flow. It addresses both degrading metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), it is the best-evidenced direction available, and memory_91's activation-messaging effect is complementary rather than competing, so nothing is lost by not running it this week. Two cautions I am carrying forward rather than resolving. First, memory_31 stayed unverified, and it is a different mechanism from exp_86: cutting required signup fields is not the same intervention as shortening the post-signup flow, and it is the variant that plausibly degrades lead qualification by admitting lower-intent accounts. I am therefore scoping this experiment to flow shortening and explicitly excluding signup field removal, so I am not silently importing an unverified and higher-risk mechanism under the same label. Second, exp_86's retention evidence stops at 30 days, and exp_73 is a live demonstration that 30-day numbers can look fine while the cohort fails at renewal. So I do not treat +3% at 30 days as proof of durable value. Instrument on qualified pipeline and 60/90-day retention, not completion rate; a completion-only lift counts as unconverted and does not justify a broad rollout. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout for that reason. Residual risk: this does nothing about the competitor's price pressure on SMB this week, and some price-sensitive accounts will be lost. That is the correct trade given exp_73 shows the discount response buys accounts that churn before renewal.

final2.rationale: Nothing in this morning's news changes the evidence, only the pressure. The competitor going deeper makes promotional_pricing feel more urgent, but exp_73 is the single most relevant record we hold and it points the other way at exactly this moment: 40% targeted discounting to price-sensitive SMB bought signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% on top of 30-day retention -12%, with the original analysts writing an explicit do-not-generalize warning. Matching a deeper cut under a sustainable-qualified-revenue objective would buy a quarter and sell the renewal cycle. Worse, the discount would now be aimed at a different population than exp_73 tested. exp_73 measured newly acquired discounted accounts; what leadership is reacting to is defensive retention of the existing SMB base. We have no verified record for defensive discounting at all, and the archive is closed, so choosing it would mean extrapolating past the one datum we have into a direction where that datum is negative. That is the weakest possible basis for the largest possible commitment. I am explicitly not treating the doubled churn conversations as evidence that discounting works; they are evidence of a problem, not of a remedy. Holding: shorten the onboarding flow, standard experiment, scoped to post-signup flow only and still excluding signup field removal, since memory_31's field-cutting mechanism remains unverified and is the variant most likely to admit low-intent accounts. exp_86 remains the best-evidenced direction and it addresses both metrics that are actually degrading under our control (completion -4%, activation -6%). Guardrails unchanged and now more important: measure qualified pipeline and 60/90-day retention, not completion rate; exp_73 is proof that healthy 30-day numbers can sit on a cohort that dies at renewal, and exp_86's retention evidence also stops at 30 days, so I am not claiming durable value has been demonstrated. Two things I want on the record rather than buried. First, the churn conversations are a real signal and this experiment does not answer them; the right response is retention and value work with those specific accounts — pricing-structure review, save motions, understanding what they are actually leaving for — which is account management this week, not the one experiment slot, and it should not be silently converted into a blanket discount. Second, next cycle's verification budget should go to whether any defensive or non-discount pricing response exists that survives a renewal cycle, since that is now the highest-consequence belief we have no support for. Residual risk accepted: we will lose price-sensitive SMB accounts this quarter that a deep cut would have held. Given the one record we have, most of those accounts would not have survived the first renewal anyway, and holding the line preserves margin and price integrity for the base that would.
